Orcasho — Integration Mechanism for Health Systems

Chronic care management for the 340 days your patients spend outside our walls.

Your health system owns the clinical encounter. Orcasho runs a continuous longitudinal feedback loop for everything that happens to a chronic patient between visits — every 20 days, on real-world outcomes, with full visibility back to the physician.

01 — The Problem

One year, divided.

A chronic patient sees their health system for roughly 25 days a year. The other 340 days, their gut environment, absorption, and medication response keep shifting — unmonitored and unadjusted. Orcasho was built to live in that second segment.

Clinical visits
Orcasho — continuous 20-day cycles
~25 days / year inside your health system ~340 days / year inside Orcasho
What Orcasho Is Optimizing For

Most chronic-care systems attempt to create stability by restricting food choices, avoiding triggers, modifying lifestyle, or repeatedly adjusting medications.

Orcasho is designed around a different objective:

Patient stability despite food variation, medication variation, hormonal changes, travel, and day-to-day life.

The goal is not perfect compliance with a rigid protocol.

The goal is maintaining a consistent physiological response under real-world conditions, even as food intake, medications, schedules, and life circumstances change.

This is why Orcasho operates in continuous 20-day feedback cycles. The protocol adapts to the patient, rather than requiring the patient to continuously adapt to the protocol.

"Patients should not need to organize their lives around their condition. The system should organize itself around the patient."
02 — The Orcasho Workflow

How a 20-day cycle runs.

Each patient is represented as a continuously updated biochemical profile. Every 20 days, the system evaluates patient feedback, clinical data, and response history, then adapts the next intervention cycle.

01 / Intake

Map the state

Symptoms, labs, medication history, and absorption signals are mapped into the patient's biochemical vector.

02 / Select

Choose the intervention

Compounds are selected by cosine similarity — directional alignment with the required ionic shift.

03 / Apply

Run the cycle

Patient follows the protocol for 20 days. No large jumps — incremental, evidence-based change.

04 / Read & adjust

Recalibrate

Response is measured, fed back into the model, and the next cycle's protocol is generated.

02 — The Orcasho Workflow · The Proprietary Dataset

We don't pull data. We build it.

Every Orcasho dataset is generated from our own closed-loop cycles — real patients, real interventions, real measured responses. Nothing is sourced, scraped, or modeled from external population data.

Source

Real-world, n-of-1 → n-of-300

Each patient runs repeated within-patient intervention cycles. The same protocol change is observed across multiple cycles in the same patient, then across patients with similar biochemical profiles.

Depth

Depth per patient, not count

Patients with 15–20 cycles over 18 months represent intervention-response depth a new entrant cannot acquire by signing up more patients faster.

Compounding

Every cycle improves the next

Outcome-linked cycles feed back into compound selection and magnitude calibration — the system gets more accurate with use, not just bigger.

The moat

Time, not data volume

20-day biological response cycles cannot be compressed. A competitor starting today needs 18+ months to reach the data depth our current patients already represent.

1. Executive Summary

Orcasho is a closed-loop biochemical control system that continuously adapts chronic care protocols every 20 days based on real patient feedback. The platform treats digestive biochemical stability as an upstream control variable for chronic disease, operating as a longitudinal care layer between episodic clinical touchpoints.

The evidence base below represents approximately 300 real-world patients treated since January 2023. This is not a randomised controlled trial. It is consistent real-world evidence of outcomes across a diverse patient population under bootstrapped, non-institutional conditions. The appropriate next step is a tightly scoped institutional pilot to evaluate deployment feasibility and whether the outcomes replicate within a health system environment.

2. Population-Level Evidence: 300 Patients

2.1 Primary Outcome — PPI and Antacid Discontinuation

96% of patients have discontinued PPIs and antacids. This is the most direct population-level signal in the evidence base. Patients did not stop PPIs because we told them to — they stopped because the upstream digestive biochemical environment stabilised to the point where acid suppression was no longer required. Acid reflux and GERD are downstream effects of an unstable gut processing environment. When digestion and absorption stabilise, the ionic and enzymatic balance that governs acid production normalises. The observed pattern suggests that stabilising the upstream digestive environment may reduce the need for acid suppression in a substantial subset of patients, rather than simply masking symptoms through pharmacological inhibition.

This is the core thesis of the Orcasho mechanism made visible in population-level data. 96% of patients across diverse demographics, conditions, and geographies showed the same pattern.

2.2 Secondary Outcome — Downstream Blood Marker Improvement

Over 70% of patients have shown positive downstream improvements in blood markers beyond their primary gut symptoms. This is the upstream control layer thesis made measurable. When digestion and absorption stabilise, medications that patients are already taking begin to absorb more consistently. Food nutrients that were previously passing through without adequate uptake begin reaching systemic circulation. The downstream effects appear in blood panels that have nothing to do with gut symptoms on their face.

Patients presenting with thyroid dysfunction show TSH movements consistent with improved medication processing through a stabilised gut environment. Patients with lipid dysregulation show HDL and LDL changes consistent with improved hepatic function. Patients with anaemia show RBC and haemoglobin movement consistent with improved B12 and folate assimilation. These patterns are observed across the patient base. The mechanistic explanation is a hypothesis, not a proven causal claim at this stage.

These are not coincidental. They are the predictable downstream consequence of stabilising the upstream digestive biochemical environment that all of these systems depend on.

3. Why These Outcomes Make Mechanistic Sense

Every input to the human body — food, medication, supplements, water — follows the same pathway: mouth, stomach acid, enzymatic hydrolysis, small intestine absorption, blood. Blood is where every clinical measurement happens. Every diagnostic number, every tracked biomarker, every medication plasma level is a downstream readout of what absorption delivered.

If the gut processing environment is unstable, downstream outputs tend to be unstable. This is the working hypothesis that the observed patient patterns support. Consistent downstream outputs cannot be produced by an inconsistent upstream process.

Current chronic care measures and manages outputs. It tracks glucose, TSH, LDL, and blood pressure. It prescribes medications to adjust those outputs. But it does not systematically stabilise the input processing layer that determines how consistently those medications and nutrients actually reach the systems they are meant to affect.

Orcasho stabilises the gut processing environment. Every 20 days the system measures where the patient's gut processing environment is and adjusts the biochemical protocol to move it toward stability. When that stabilisation occurs, the medications the patient is already taking work more consistently, the nutrients they are already consuming absorb more fully, and the downstream markers reflect both.

The observed outcomes are consistent with the hypothesis that stabilizing digestive processing may improve downstream physiological function.

6. Proposed Pilot Design

6.1 Objective

To evaluate whether Orcasho can function as a structured longitudinal care layer for chronic patients within a health system environment, and to measure whether the downstream improvement pattern observed across 300 real-world patients replicates within a defined institutional pilot cohort over a 9-month observation window.

6.2 Proposed Patient Cohort

CriterionSpecification
Primary complaintPersistent GI dysfunction: reflux, bloating, constipation, or upper GI instability
DurationSymptoms present 6 months or more with incomplete resolution through standard care
Medication contextCurrently on PPIs, antacids, or other GI medications without full symptom resolution
Age range18 to 70 years
ComorbiditiesMay include thyroid, metabolic, post-treatment profiles. Not excluded.
ExclusionAcute GI emergency, active malignancy under treatment, pregnancy

6.3 Pilot Size and Duration

Cohort size: 30 to 50 patients. Recommended pilot window: 9 months (approximately 270 days). Thirteen to fourteen complete 20-day adaptation cycles per patient.

Why 9 months and not 90 days: Our own patient data shows that directional movement in symptoms begins within the first 60 to 90 days. Meaningful blood marker stabilization consistently requires 6 to 9 months. The average patient in our current base stays 9 to 18 months precisely because the outcomes compound over time. A 90-day pilot can evaluate workflow feasibility but cannot evaluate the downstream biochemical outcomes that represent the core clinical claim. Designing a pilot shorter than the period where outcomes become visible produces incomplete and potentially misleading results.

Observation cadence: every 3 months within the 9-month window.

CheckpointFocus
Month 3Workflow feasibility, early symptom signal, initial directional movement
Month 6Medication change patterns, first blood marker trends
Month 9Full outcome picture across all endpoints

Location: Home-based throughout. No clinic visits required for the Orcasho protocol layer. Physician dashboard: Full visibility at all times. Clinical team can review, intervene, or escalate at any point.

6.4 Endpoints

EndpointTypeMeasurement
Symptom stabilizationPrimaryPatient-reported score at baseline, month 3, month 6, month 9
PPI and antacid usagePrimaryChange in medication dependency tracked every 3 months
Downstream markersSecondaryAvailable blood markers at baseline, month 3, month 6, month 9
Patient retentionOperationalPercentage completing full 9-month window
Adverse eventsSafetyAny adverse responses during the pilot
Workflow feasibilityOperationalDashboard engagement and escalation rate
Proposed Pilot in Brief

30 to 50 patients with persistent chronic GI burden. 9-month observation window. Thirteen to fourteen 20-day adaptation cycles. Assessment at months 3, 6, and 9. Home-based throughout. Physician dashboard with full visibility. Primary endpoints: symptom stabilization and PPI/antacid usage change tracked every 3 months. Secondary: downstream blood marker trends at each assessment point. No clinical visits required for the Orcasho protocol layer. Duration aligned with how biology actually moves, not institutional convenience.

Appendix — Ionic Model · Vector Mathematics · Cosine Similarity

Inside one cycle: how the next protocol gets chosen.

Symptom severities (GERD, constipation, bloating) are converted into a 15-dimensional ionic target vector. Every compound in the library is scored against that target by cosine similarity and Euclidean distance — the highest-ranked compounds form the next protocol.

Resolution equation — the biochemical "why"
↑ ATP· ↓ H+· ↑ HCO3−· ↑ Na+/K+-ATPase· ↑ LES pressure → ↑ Cl−/Mg2+ flux· ↑ motility· ↓ ROS → ↓ CO2· ↑ HCO3−· ↑ Na+/Cl− motility

This equation is what's read back into the next protocol: a directional correction on the patient's biochemical state — not a fixed dose schedule.

Appendix — Neural Network Diagram · The Replication Problem

70–100 supplement compounds. One combination, every 20 days.

Every 20-day cycle, the full library of 70–100 supplement compounds is passed through the 15-dimensional ionic equilibrium model against that patient's latest feedback. The model resolves to one specific combination — for this patient, this cycle, it converged on Digestive Enzymes + Probiotics + L-Theanine + L-Glycine + Zinc. Next cycle, the same 70–100 compounds are re-evaluated against new feedback, and a different combination emerges. The number of possible patient-specific, cycle-specific combinations is enormous — and each one is only correct because of the within-patient history behind it. That history is what can't be bought or copied; it can only be accumulated, one cycle at a time.

Same 70–100 compounds, same 15-dimensional model — but a different feedback input next cycle resolves to a different combination. A competitor with the same supplement library and the same model still lacks the only thing that determines which combination is correct for this patient, right now: the accumulated history of what their body did the last 12 times something changed.

Appendix — Compound Selection Logic

A control variable, not a symptom.

Most approaches to gut dysfunction treat it as a symptom to suppress — acid blockers, antacids, dietary restriction. Orcasho's founder approached it differently: as a control variable sitting upstream of nearly every chronic symptom, governed by feedback loops rather than fixed protocols.

The reframe

Symptom → control variable

That single shift — from "what do we treat" to "what do we adjust" — is what makes a feedback loop possible instead of a static prescription.

The training

Fundamental chemistry, not clinical protocol

Clinicians are trained to identify and treat. A chemistry background trains you to identify and model — to represent a system as state variables that can be measured, perturbed, and read back.

The architecture

15-dimensional state, ionic alignment

Each patient is modeled as a 15-dimensional biochemical vector. Interventions are selected by cosine similarity — directional alignment with the ionic shift the patient's data calls for.

The result

A control system that happens to involve biology

Adaptation isn't an add-on feature — it's the core of the architecture. That's the combination — chemistry plus control-systems thinking — now running across 300 patients.
